common_part.cm4_title: Neuroanatomical heterogeneity and homogeneity in individuals at clinical high risk for psychosis

cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.reason: The paper explicitly states its objectives and hypotheses in the introduction. It clearly outlines the aim to investigate neuroanatomical heterogeneity in CHR-P individuals compared to HCs and in relation to psychosis transition. The paper also details the rationale, mentioning the development of precision and predictive models and identifying individuals with shared characteristics, which aligns with the application purposes of normative modeling.
cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.supporting_text: Here, we aimed to apply both group-level and personalised indices to investigate whether neuroanatomical heterogeneity differed signiﬁcantly between; (i) individuals at CHR-P and HC, and (ii) individuals at CHR-P who subsequently transitioned to psychosis and those who did not. ... Speciﬁcally, we hypothesised that individuals at CHR-P will demonstrate signiﬁcantly increased heterogeneity in neuroanatomical measures, as demonstrated by signiﬁcantly higher VR effect sizes and signiﬁcantly lower PBSI scores. and The rationale for elucidating neuroanatomical heterogeneity in the context of CHR is four-fold. First, by examining neuroanatomical heterogeneity in CHR-P, we will gain a fuller understanding of neuroanatomy of the CHR-P population... Then, this increased understanding may inform the development of precision and predictive models of psychosis. Third, modelling neuroanatomical heterogeneity offers a unique opportunity to identify individuals with potentially shared characteristics of importance.
cm6_clarity_of_research_objectives.location: Baldwin2022.pdf.md: Main Manuscript / Introduction / Paragraph 4 and 5

common_part.cm7_additional_comments: This study is a large-scale mega-analysis from the ENIGMA CHR-P consortium, investigating neuroanatomical heterogeneity using both group-level (Variability Ratio, Coefficient of Variation Ratio) and individual-level (Person-Based Similarity Index) approaches. The PBSI was used to assess both within-group similarity and individual deviation from a normative (healthy control) profile.

nm1_clear_definition_of_target_populatio.reason: The study uses the existing ENIGMA CHR-P dataset. The paper clearly describes the demographic characteristics (age, sex) of both the CHR-P and HC groups in Table 1. It specifies that CHR-P criteria were met according to CAARMS or SIPS. The reason for selecting this dataset is also explicitly stated: it is the largest pooled structural neuroimaging CHR-P dataset, offering a unique opportunity to investigate heterogeneity.
nm1_clear_definition_of_target_populatio.supporting_text: The ENIGMA CHR-P dataset amalgamated clinical and neuroimaging data from 29 sites, comprising 1579 individuals meeting CHR-P criteria (according to Comprehensive Assessment of At-Risk Mental States [CAARMS] [9] or the Structured Interview for Prodromal Syndromes [SIPS] [39, 40]) and 1243 HC participants. (from Methods/Participants). Table 1 shows age and sex data. The ENIGMA [25] consortium offers rich structural neuroimaging data across a diverse sample at CHR-P [20], and therefore presents a unique opportunity to systematically address the issue of heterogeneity in this population. (from Introduction).

Further regression models also adjusted for age and sex.

nm7_clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.reason: The study clearly describes its data partitioning for the normative modeling analysis. The entire Healthy Control (HC) group (N=1243) was used as the reference/training set to build the normative model, and the entire Clinical High Risk for Psychosis (CHR-P) group (N=1579) was used as the test set. This partitioning is based on the clinical diagnosis of the participants. This method inherently prevents data leakage as the training and test sets are fully independent. No cross-validation or further partitioning was mentioned as it was not applicable to this design.
nm7_clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.supporting_text: (ii) Normative reference: Next, the respective neuroanatomical proﬁles of each CHR-P individual were correlated with the corresponding proﬁles of the members of the HC group, for each brain phenotype. The resulting PBSI scores thus represent the degree of deviation from the 'normative' range and were transformed into z-scores (PBSI-CT-Z, PBSI-SA-Z, and PBSI-SV-Z).

nm8_details_of_normative_modeling_approa.reason: The paper provides a detailed description of its normative modeling approach, the Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI). The statistical method, which is based on calculating the average Spearman correlation between an individual's brain profile and the profiles of a reference group, is clearly specified. The settings, such as the brain phenotypes used (SA, CT, SV) and the choice of the HC group as the normative reference, are described. The software used for the analyses (R v.4.0.3) is mentioned, and while a specific package for PBSI is not named, the paper provides the formula and states that the code is available upon request, suggesting a custom implementation.
nm8_details_of_normative_modeling_approa.supporting_text: The personalised estimates of interindividual variability were investigated using the PBSI, calculated according to the formula below, for each SA, CT and SV proﬁles... The PBSI of the i th individual is the average correlation between his/her brain measures ( yi ) and the brain measures of any other individual of the reference sample ( yj , for j ≠ i )... Spearman correlation coefﬁcients were computed... All analyses were conducted within R v .4.0.3

nm9_details_of_training_algorithm.reason: The normative modeling approach used in this study, the Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI), is a descriptive statistical method based on Spearman correlations. It does not involve an iterative training algorithm with optimization processes, hyperparameters, or convergence criteria like those found in machine learning models (e.g., gradient descent, ADAM). The PBSI is calculated directly from the data. Therefore, the concept of a 'training algorithm' as described in the assessment criteria is not applicable to this study's methodology.

nm10_model_performance_evaluation_metric.reason: The study does not evaluate its normative model using traditional performance metrics like R² or MSLL because the PBSI is a descriptive, not a predictive, model. However, it thoroughly evaluates the model's output. The primary metrics are the Variability Ratio (VR) and the Person-Based Similarity Index (PBSI) score itself. The paper clearly explains the meaning and interpretation of these metrics. It details the methods for evaluating statistical significance, using FDR-corrected p-values for VR and Welch's t-tests and regression models for PBSI. Point estimates (VRs, group means for PBSI, regression coefficients), confidence intervals (for VR), and p-values are all reported appropriately in the text and figures. While not a typical performance evaluation, it is a comprehensive evaluation suitable for the chosen methodology.
nm10_model_performance_evaluation_metric.supporting_text: A VR > 1 suggests greater variability in the CHR-P group... A higher PBSI score (closer to 1) indicates greater similarity... Group-level comparisons of PBSI-SA, PBSI-CT and PBSI-SV were then conducted between CHRP and HC using one-tailed Welch ' s t tests... we calculated p value adjustments using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) approach...
